question: Can you list for me all the usa secretaries of education from the beginning of 2018 until the end of 2024? including short acting secretaries
response:
Here are the United States Secretaries of Education (including Acting Secretaries) who served from **January 1, 2018**, through **December 31, 2024**.

*   **Betsy DeVos**
    *   **Role:** 11th Secretary of Education
    *   **Dates:** Served the entire period from **January 1, 2018** until her resignation on **January 8, 2021**.
    *   *(Originally sworn in February 7, 2017)*

*   **Mitchell "Mick" Zais**
    *   **Role:** Acting Secretary
    *   **Dates:** **January 8, 2021 – January 20, 2021**
    *   *Note:* Assumed the role following DeVos's resignation shortly before the inauguration of President Biden.

*   **Phil Rosenfelt**
    *   **Role:** Acting Secretary
    *   **Dates:** **January 20, 2021 – March 2, 2021**
    *   *Note:* A career official designated to lead the department during the transition period until a permanent secretary was confirmed.

*   **Miguel Cardona**
    *   **Role:** 12th Secretary of Education
    *   **Dates:** **March 2, 2021 – December 31, 2024** (continued serving into 2025)
    *   *Note:* Confirmed by the Senate regarding the Biden Administration's appointment.

*   **Role:** 11th United States Secretary of Education
*   **Term in Period:** January 1, 2018 – January 8, 2021
*   **Note:** Secretary DeVos was appointed by President Donald Trump and confirmed in February 2017. She served continuously through 2018, 2019, and 2020. She resigned on January 7, 2021 (effective January 8) following the riots at the U.S. Capitol.

*   **Role:** Acting United States Secretary of Education
*   **Term:** January 8, 2021 – January 20, 2021
*   **Note:** Zais served as the Deputy Secretary of Education under Betsy DeVos. Following her resignation, he assumed the role of Acting Secretary until the end of the Trump administration at noon on Inauguration Day.

*   **Role:** Acting United States Secretary of Education
*   **Term:** January 20, 2021 – March 2, 2021
*   **Note:** A career official and the Department's Deputy General Counsel, Rosenfelt was designated by President Joe Biden to serve as Acting Secretary immediately following his inauguration to lead the agency during the transition period until a permanent secretary was confirmed.

### **4. Miguel Cardona**
*   **Role:** 12th United States Secretary of Education
*   **Term:** March 2, 2021 – Present (Served through the end of 2024)
*   **Note:** Appointed by President Joe Biden, Dr. Cardona was confirmed by the Senate on March 1, 2021, and sworn in on March 2, 2021. He served as Secretary for the remainder of the period requested (2021–2024).

**1. Rex Tillerson**
*   **Role:** 69th Secretary of State
*   **Tenure within Period:** January 1, 2018 – March 31, 2018

**2. John Sullivan**
*   **Role:** Acting Secretary of State
*   **Tenure:** April 1, 2018 – April 26, 2018
*   **Notes:** Sullivan, then the Deputy Secretary of State, assumed the role of Acting Secretary following Tillerson's departure and served until Mike Pompeo was confirmed and sworn in.

**3. Mike Pompeo**
*   **Role:** 70th Secretary of State
*   **Tenure:** April 26, 2018 – January 20, 2021
*   **Notes:** Pompeo was sworn in on April 26, 2018, and served until the end of the Trump administration at noon on Inauguration Day, 2021.

**4. Daniel Smith**
*   **Role:** Acting Secretary of State
*   **Tenure:** January 20, 2021 – January 26, 2021
*   **Notes:** A career diplomat and former Director of the Foreign Service Institute, Smith was appointed by President Biden to serve as Acting Secretary on Inauguration Day while the Senate considered Antony Blinken's nomination.

**5. Antony Blinken**
*   **Role:** 71st Secretary of State
*   **Tenure:** January 26, 2021 – Present (as of December 2024)
*   **Notes:** Blinken was confirmed by the Senate and sworn in on January 26, 2021. He served throughout the remainder of the period (through Dec 2024).

*   **Appointed by:** Joe Biden

This is a **list of secretaries of state of the United States**.

## Secretaries of foreign affairs (1781–1789)

On January 10, 1780, the [Congress of the Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_the_Confederation "Congress of the Confederation") created the Department of Foreign Affairs.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_secretaries_of_state#cite_note-1)

On August 10, 1781, Congress selected [Robert R. Livingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_R._Livingston "Robert R. Livingston"), a delegate from [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"), as the first secretary for foreign affairs. Livingston was unable to take office until October 20, 1781. He served until June 4, 1783, and was succeeded by [Elias Boudinot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elias_Boudinot "Elias Boudinot"), who was succeeded by [John Jay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jay "John Jay") on December 21, 1784, who served until March 4, 1789, when the government under the [Articles of Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Articles_of_Confederation "Articles of Confederation") gave way to the government under the [Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_United_States "Constitution of the United States").

The office of secretary of foreign affairs and the Department of Foreign Affairs were reinstated by a law signed by [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington") on July 27, 1789. [John Jay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jay "John Jay") retained the post on an interim basis, pending the return of [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") from France.

## Secretaries of state

On September 15, 1789, before Jefferson could return to take the post, Washington signed into law another act which changed the name of the office from Secretary of Foreign Affairs to [Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State"), changed the name of the department to the [Department of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State "United States Department of State"), and added several domestic powers and responsibilities to both the office of secretary and the department. [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") took office as the first secretary of state on March 22, 1790.

This is a list of United States secretaries of state by time in office. This is based on the difference between dates; if counted by number of calendar days all the figures would be one greater. [Cordell Hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordell_Hull "Cordell Hull") is the only person to have served as secretary of state for more than eight years. [Daniel Webster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Webster "Daniel Webster") and [James G. Blaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_G._Blaine "James G. Blaine") are the only secretaries of state to have ever served non-consecutive terms. [Warren Christopher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Christopher "Warren Christopher") served very briefly as acting secretary of state non-consecutively with his later tenure as full-fledged secretary of state. [Elihu B. Washburne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elihu_B._Washburne "Elihu B. Washburne") served as secretary of state for less than two weeks before becoming [ambassador to France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_France "List of ambassadors of the United States to France").

The US Secretaries of State and Acting Secretaries who served between January 2018 and December 2024 are listed chronologically below.

This period spanned the presidencies of Donald Trump and Joe Biden and included two Senate-confirmed Secretaries of State and two Acting Secretaries.

### **1. Rex Tillerson**
*   **Role:** 69th Secretary of State
*   **Tenure during period:** January 1, 2018 – March 31, 2018
*   **Appointed by:** Donald Trump
*   **Notes:** Secretary Tillerson served from February 1, 2017, until his term officially ended on March 31, 2018. President Trump announced his dismissal on March 13, 2018, but he retained the title until the end of the month, though he delegated all authorities to Deputy Secretary John Sullivan during his final weeks.

### **2. John Sullivan (Acting)**
*   **Role:** Acting Secretary of State
*   **Tenure:** April 1, 2018 – April 26, 2018
*   **Appointed by:** Served by virtue of his position as Deputy Secretary of State.
*   **Notes:** Sullivan became the Acting Secretary following Tillerson's official departure and served until Mike Pompeo was sworn in.

### **3. Mike Pompeo**
*   **Role:** 70th Secretary of State
*   **Tenure:** April 26, 2018 – January 20, 2021
*   **Appointed by:** Donald Trump
*   **Notes:** Pompeo served until the end of the Trump administration. He left office at noon on inauguration day.

### **4. Daniel Bennett Smith (Acting)**
*   **Role:** Acting Secretary of State
*   **Tenure:** January 20, 2021 – January 26, 2021
*   **Appointed by:** Joe Biden
*   **Notes:** A career Foreign Service officer and former Director of the Foreign Service Institute, Smith was appointed by President Biden to serve as Acting Secretary immediately following the inauguration while the Senate considered Antony Blinken's nomination.

### **5. Antony Blinken**
*   **Role:** 71st Secretary of State
*   **Tenure:** January 26, 2021 – December 31, 2024 (Continued into 2025)
*   **Appointed by:** Joe Biden
*   **Notes:** Blinken was confirmed by the Senate and sworn in on January 26, 2021. He served through the remainder of the period in question.

This is a **list of secretaries of state of the United States**.

## Secretaries of foreign affairs (1781–1789)

On January 10, 1780, the [Congress of the Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_the_Confederation "Congress of the Confederation") created the Department of Foreign Affairs.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_secretaries_of_state#cite_note-1)

On August 10, 1781, Congress selected [Robert R. Livingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_R._Livingston "Robert R. Livingston"), a delegate from [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"), as the first secretary for foreign affairs. Livingston was unable to take office until October 20, 1781. He served until June 4, 1783, and was succeeded by [Elias Boudinot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elias_Boudinot "Elias Boudinot"), who was succeeded by [John Jay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jay "John Jay") on December 21, 1784, who served until March 4, 1789, when the government under the [Articles of Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Articles_of_Confederation "Articles of Confederation") gave way to the government under the [Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_United_States "Constitution of the United States").

The office of secretary of foreign affairs and the Department of Foreign Affairs were reinstated by a law signed by [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington") on July 27, 1789. [John Jay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jay "John Jay") retained the post on an interim basis, pending the return of [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") from France.

This is a list of United States secretaries of state by time in office. This is based on the difference between dates; if counted by number of calendar days all the figures would be one greater. [Cordell Hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordell_Hull "Cordell Hull") is the only person to have served as secretary of state for more than eight years. [Daniel Webster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Webster "Daniel Webster") and [James G. Blaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_G._Blaine "James G. Blaine") are the only secretaries of state to have ever served non-consecutive terms. [Warren Christopher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Christopher "Warren Christopher") served very briefly as acting secretary of state non-consecutively with his later tenure as full-fledged secretary of state. [Elihu B. Washburne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elihu_B._Washburne "Elihu B. Washburne") served as secretary of state for less than two weeks before becoming [ambassador to France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_France "List of ambassadors of the United States to France").

Here is the list of United States Secretaries of State, including acting secretaries, who served from the beginning of 2018 through the end of 2024:

**1. Rex Tillerson**
*   **Role:** 69th Secretary of State
*   **Dates Served in Period:** Jan 1, 2018 – Mar 31, 2018
*   **Note:** Although dismissed by President Trump mid-March, he officially held the office until the end of the month, delegating duties to Deputy Secretary John Sullivan during his final weeks.

**2. John J. Sullivan** (Acting)
*   **Role:** Acting Secretary of State
*   **Dates Served:** Apr 1, 2018 – Apr 26, 2018
*   **Note:** Automatically assumed the role of Acting Secretary upon Tillerson's departure by virtue of being the Deputy Secretary of State.

**3. Mike Pompeo**
*   **Role:** 70th Secretary of State
*   **Dates Served:** Apr 26, 2018 – Jan 20, 2021
*   **Note:** Served until the end of the Trump administration.

**4. Daniel Bennett Smith** (Acting)
*   **Role:** Acting Secretary of State
*   **Dates Served:** Jan 20, 2021 – Jan 26, 2021
*   **Note:** A career Foreign Service officer appointed by President Biden to serve temporarily during the transition while the Senate considered Antony Blinken's nomination.

**5. Antony Blinken**
*   **Role:** 71st Secretary of State
*   **Dates Served:** Jan 26, 2021 – End of 2024 (and continuing)
*   **Note:** Confirmed by the Senate and sworn in shortly after the start of the Biden administration.

This is a **list of secretaries of state of the United States**.

## Secretaries of foreign affairs (1781–1789)

On January 10, 1780, the [Congress of the Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_the_Confederation "Congress of the Confederation") created the Department of Foreign Affairs.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_secretaries_of_state#cite_note-1)

On August 10, 1781, Congress selected [Robert R. Livingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_R._Livingston "Robert R. Livingston"), a delegate from [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"), as the first secretary for foreign affairs. Livingston was unable to take office until October 20, 1781. He served until June 4, 1783, and was succeeded by [Elias Boudinot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elias_Boudinot "Elias Boudinot"), who was succeeded by [John Jay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jay "John Jay") on December 21, 1784, who served until March 4, 1789, when the government under the [Articles of Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Articles_of_Confederation "Articles of Confederation") gave way to the government under the [Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_United_States "Constitution of the United States").

The office of secretary of foreign affairs and the Department of Foreign Affairs were reinstated by a law signed by [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington") on July 27, 1789. [John Jay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jay "John Jay") retained the post on an interim basis, pending the return of [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") from France.

## Secretaries of state

On September 15, 1789, before Jefferson could return to take the post, Washington signed into law another act which changed the name of the office from Secretary of Foreign Affairs to [Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State"), changed the name of the department to the [Department of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State "United States Department of State"), and added several domestic powers and responsibilities to both the office of secretary and the department. [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") took office as the first secretary of state on March 22, 1790.

This is a list of United States secretaries of state by time in office. This is based on the difference between dates; if counted by number of calendar days all the figures would be one greater. [Cordell Hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordell_Hull "Cordell Hull") is the only person to have served as secretary of state for more than eight years. [Daniel Webster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Webster "Daniel Webster") and [James G. Blaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_G._Blaine "James G. Blaine") are the only secretaries of state to have ever served non-consecutive terms. [Warren Christopher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Christopher "Warren Christopher") served very briefly as acting secretary of state non-consecutively with his later tenure as full-fledged secretary of state. [Elihu B. Washburne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elihu_B._Washburne "Elihu B. Washburne") served as secretary of state for less than two weeks before becoming [ambassador to France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_France "List of ambassadors of the United States to France").

This is a **list of secretaries of state of the United States**.

## Secretaries of foreign affairs (1781–1789)

On January 10, 1780, the [Congress of the Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_the_Confederation "Congress of the Confederation") created the Department of Foreign Affairs.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_secretaries_of_state#cite_note-1)

On August 10, 1781, Congress selected [Robert R. Livingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_R._Livingston "Robert R. Livingston"), a delegate from [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"), as the first secretary for foreign affairs. Livingston was unable to take office until October 20, 1781. He served until June 4, 1783, and was succeeded by [Elias Boudinot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elias_Boudinot "Elias Boudinot"), who was succeeded by [John Jay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jay "John Jay") on December 21, 1784, who served until March 4, 1789, when the government under the [Articles of Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Articles_of_Confederation "Articles of Confederation") gave way to the government under the [Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_United_States "Constitution of the United States").

The office of secretary of foreign affairs and the Department of Foreign Affairs were reinstated by a law signed by [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington") on July 27, 1789. [John Jay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jay "John Jay") retained the post on an interim basis, pending the return of [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") from France.

## Secretaries of state

On September 15, 1789, before Jefferson could return to take the post, Washington signed into law another act which changed the name of the office from Secretary of Foreign Affairs to [Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State"), changed the name of the department to the [Department of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State "United States Department of State"), and added several domestic powers and responsibilities to both the office of secretary and the department. [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") took office as the first secretary of state on March 22, 1790.

This is a list of United States secretaries of state by time in office. This is based on the difference between dates; if counted by number of calendar days all the figures would be one greater. [Cordell Hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordell_Hull "Cordell Hull") is the only person to have served as secretary of state for more than eight years. [Daniel Webster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Webster "Daniel Webster") and [James G. Blaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_G._Blaine "James G. Blaine") are the only secretaries of state to have ever served non-consecutive terms. [Warren Christopher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Christopher "Warren Christopher") served very briefly as acting secretary of state non-consecutively with his later tenure as full-fledged secretary of state. [Elihu B. Washburne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elihu_B._Washburne "Elihu B. Washburne") served as secretary of state for less than two weeks before becoming [ambassador to France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_France "List of ambassadors of the United States to France").

Here are the United States Secretaries of Commerce who served from the beginning of 2018 through the end of 2024, including those who served in an acting capacity.

### **Timeline (2018–2024)**

**1. Wilbur Ross**
*   **Role:** 39th Secretary of Commerce
*   **Dates in requested period:** January 1, 2018 – January 20, 2021
*   **Note:** Appointed by Donald Trump, he entered office in February 2017 and served until the end of the term.

**2. Wynn Coggins**
*   **Role:** Acting Secretary of Commerce
*   **Dates:** January 20, 2021 – March 3, 2021
*   **Note:** A career civil servant (Deputy Assistant Secretary for Administration), Coggins served as the acting head of the department during the transition period between the Trump and Biden administrations until a permanent nominee could be confirmed.

**3. Gina Raimondo**
*   **Role:** 40th Secretary of Commerce
*   **Dates:** March 3, 2021 – December 31, 2024
*   **Note:** Appointed by Joe Biden, she was sworn in on March 3, 2021, and served through the end of 2024 (and remains in office).

message.content:
Here are the United States Secretaries of Commerce who served from the beginning of 2018 through the end of 2024, including those who served in an acting capacity.

### **Timeline (2018–2024)**

**1. Wilbur Ross**
*   **Role:** 39th Secretary of Commerce
*   **Dates in requested period:** January 1, 2018 – January 20, 2021
*   **Note:** Appointed by Donald Trump, he entered office in February 2017 and served until the end of the term.

**2. Wynn Coggins**
*   **Role:** Acting Secretary of Commerce
*   **Dates:** January 20, 2021 – March 3, 2021
*   **Note:** A career civil servant (Deputy Assistant Secretary for Administration), Coggins served as the acting head of the department during the transition period between the Trump and Biden administrations until a permanent nominee could be confirmed.

**3. Gina Raimondo**

    *   **Dates of Service:** January 20, 2021 – February 25, 2021

### **List of US Secretaries of Energy (2017–2025)**

| Name | Role | Term Start | Term End | Administration |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

| **Rick Perry** | Secretary | March 2, 2017 | December 1, 2019 | Trump |

| **David Huizenga** | Acting Secretary | January 20, 2021 | February 25, 2021 | Biden |
| **Jennifer Granholm** | Secretary | February 25, 2021 | January 20, 2025 | Biden |
| **Ingrid Kolb** | Acting Secretary | January 20, 2025 | February 3, 2025 | Trump (2nd Term) |
| **Chris Wright** | Secretary | February 3, 2025 | *Present* | Trump (2nd Term) |

***

### **Detailed Timeline**

#### **Trump Administration (First Term)**
*   **Grace Bochenek (Acting):** A career official who served as Acting Secretary immediately following the inauguration of Donald Trump until his nominee was confirmed.
*   **Rick Perry:** Confirmed by the Senate on March 2, 2017. He announced his resignation in late 2019 and left office on December 1, 2019.
*   **Dan Brouillette:** Served as Deputy Secretary under Perry. He became Acting Secretary upon Perry's resignation. He was confirmed by the Senate on December 2, 2019, and officially sworn in on December 11, 2019. He served until the end of the term.

#### **Biden Administration**
*   **David Huizenga (Acting):** A career official (Associate Administrator for the National Nuclear Security Administration) who served as Acting Secretary during the transition while Jennifer Granholm awaited confirmation.
*   **Jennifer Granholm:** Confirmed by the Senate on February 25, 2021, and sworn in shortly after. She served through the end of President Biden's term on January 20, 2025.

#### **Trump Administration (Second Term)**
*   **Ingrid Kolb (Acting):** A Department of Energy official who served as Acting Secretary during the transition period beginning January 20, 2025.
*   **Chris Wright:** CEO of Liberty Energy and Trump's nominee for Energy Secretary. He was confirmed by the Senate and sworn in on February 3, 2025.

Based on the official records and transition timelines for the U.S. Department of Commerce between **2018 and 2024**, there were **no other Acting U.S. Secretaries of Commerce** besides **Wynn Coggins**.

**Wynn Coggins** was the sole Acting Secretary during this period, serving during the transition between the Trump and Biden administrations.

### Timeline of Leadership (2018–2024)

*   **Wilbur Ross (Secretary):** Served from February 28, 2017, until January 20, 2021.
    *   *Note:* Ross remained in office throughout the entirety of 2018, 2019, and 2020.
*   **Wynn Coggins (Acting Secretary):** Served from **January 20, 2021**, to **March 3, 2021**.
    *   A career civil servant (Deputy Assistant Secretary for Administration), Coggins was designated by President Biden to lead the department immediately following his inauguration until a permanent secretary could be confirmed.
*   **Gina Raimondo (Secretary):** Sworn in on **March 3, 2021**, and served through the end of 2024.
    *   *Note:* Secretary Raimondo held the office continuously from her swearing-in without a vacancy that would require an Acting Secretary.

### Additional Context
While other officials like **Karen Dunn Kelley** served as Deputy Secretary (2018–2021) and may have performed the duties of the Secretary during short absences, they did not hold the title of Acting Secretary due to a vacancy in the office. **Jeremy Pelter** is listed as an Acting Secretary starting **January 20, 2025**, which falls outside the 2018–2024 window you specified.

The following is the list of United States Secretaries of Health and Human Services (HHS) who served between 2018 and 2024, including those who served in an acting capacity.

### **List of Secretaries of Health and Human Services (2018–2024)**

**1. Eric Hargan (Acting)**
*   **Tenure:** October 10, 2017 – January 29, 2018
*   **Appointed by:** Donald Trump
*   **Notes:** Hargan served as Acting Secretary following the resignation of Tom Price and the brief interim service of Don J. Wright. He led the department into 2018 until Alex Azar was confirmed.

**2. Alex Azar**
*   **Tenure:** January 29, 2018 – January 20, 2021
*   **Appointed by:** Donald Trump
*   **Notes:** Azar was confirmed by the Senate on January 24, 2018, and sworn in on January 29. He served for the remainder of the Trump administration, leading the department during the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic.

**3. Norris Cochran (Acting)**
*   **Tenure:** January 20, 2021 – March 19, 2021
*   **Appointed by:** Joe Biden
*   **Notes:** A career official and the Deputy Assistant Secretary (Budget), Cochran was designated Acting Secretary by President Biden upon his inauguration to lead the department while Xavier Becerra awaited Senate confirmation.

**4. Xavier Becerra**
*   **Tenure:** March 19, 2021 – Present (Served through the end of 2024)
*   **Appointed by:** Joe Biden
*   **Notes:** Becerra was confirmed by the Senate on March 18, 2021, and sworn in on March 19, 2021. He became the first Latino to hold the office and served as Secretary through the entirety of the 2021–2024 period.

*   **Term in Period:** March 19, 2021 – December 31, 2024
*   **Role:** Secretary

full_history.response:
**No, an "Acting Secretary of Transportation" did not legally take over during Pete Buttigieg's paternity leave in 2021.**

While Secretary Buttigieg was on leave following the birth of his twins in August 2021, the **Deputy Secretary of Transportation, Polly Trottenberg**, assumed the day-to-day leadership of the department. This is standard procedure for the Deputy Secretary, who serves as the department's "chief operating officer."

However, she did **not** assume the title of "Acting Secretary." That title is typically reserved for instances when the office of the Secretary is vacant (e.g., due to resignation, death, or dismissal) or during a transition between administrations.

**Key details about the arrangement:**
*   **Continued Involvement:** Secretary Buttigieg did not completely unplug. His office stated that while he was on leave, he remained available for major decisions and urgent matters.
*   **Delegation:** Deputy Secretary Trottenberg handled logistical and operational duties and represented the department at public events, but the ultimate authority remained participating with Buttigieg for high-level crises (such as the supply chain issues occurring at the time).
*   **Confusion with later roles:** You may have seen headlines about Polly Trottenberg serving as an "Acting" official, but that occurred later in **2023**, when she was designated as the **Acting Administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)**, a separate role within the DOT.

full_history.response:
Here is the list of US Secretaries of Transportation and Acting Secretaries who served between January 1, 2018, and December 31, 2024.

### **List of US Secretaries of Transportation (2018–2024)**

| Name | Role | Start Date | End Date |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Elaine Chao** | Secretary | January 31, 2017* | January 11, 2021 |
| **Steven G. Bradbury** | Acting Secretary | January 12, 2021 | January 20, 2021 |
| **Lana Hurdle** | Acting Secretary | January 20, 2021 | February 3, 2021 |
| **Pete Buttigieg** | Secretary | February 3, 2021 | *Incumbent (Serving through Dec 31, 2024)* |

*\*Elaine Chao was sworn in on January 31, 2017, and was serving at the start of the requested period (January 1, 2018).*

***

### **Detailed Timeline & Context**

*   **Elaine Chao**
    *   **Tenure:** Served under the Trump Administration.
    *   **Departure:** She was the first Cabinet secretary to resign following the events at the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021. Her resignation became effective on **January 11, 2021**.

*   **Steven G. Bradbury**
    *   **Tenure:** Served as Acting Secretary for the final days of the Trump Administration.
    *   **Context:** Bradbury was the General Counsel of the Department of Transportation who had also been performing the duties of the Deputy Secretary. He assumed the role of Acting Secretary immediately following Chao's departure on **January 12, 2021**, and served until the inauguration of Joe Biden on January 20, 2021.

*   **Lana Hurdle**
    *   **Tenure:** Served as Acting Secretary during the transition to the Biden Administration.
    *   **Context:** A career civil servant and Deputy Assistant Secretary for Budget and Programs, Hurdle was designated Acting Secretary by President Biden on inauguration day, **January 20, 2021**, to lead the department until a permanent secretary was confirmed. She served until Pete Buttigieg was sworn in.

*   **Pete Buttigieg**
    *   **Tenure:** Serving under the Biden Administration.
    *   **Context:** Confirmed by the Senate on February 2, 2021, and sworn in by Vice President Kamala Harris on **February 3, 2021**. He served continuously through the end of the requested period (December 31, 2024). While he took paternity leave in late 2021, he remained the Secretary of Transportation during that time (Deputy Secretary Polly Trottenberg handled day-to-day operations, but was not designated as "Acting Secretary").

Based on official records and public statements from that period, **Polly Trottenberg did not officially hold the title of Acting Secretary of Transportation** during Pete Buttigieg's paternity leave in 2021.

During Buttigieg's four-week leave following the birth of his twins (which began in mid-August 2021), he remained the Secretary of Transportation. As the Senate-confirmed **Deputy Secretary of Transportation**, Trottenberg assumed the day-to-day responsibilities and leadership of the department, described in reports as "taking the reins" or "filling in."

However, because Buttigieg did not resign or become permanently "unable to perform the functions and duties of the office" (which triggers the Federal Vacancies Reform Act), the position of Secretary was not legally vacant. Consequently, Trottenberg continued to serve under her official title of Deputy Secretary while performing the duties of the Secretary.

Secretary Buttigieg addressed this distinction directly in an October 2021 interview on *CNN's State of the Union*. When asked, "Why did you not appoint an acting secretary while you were away?", he responded by explaining the standard role of the Deputy Secretary to handle operations in his absence, confirming that no "Acting Secretary" was appointed.

*   **Note:** A career civil servant appointed by President Biden on Inauguration Day to manage the department until a permanent secretary could be confirmed.

### **4. Pete Buttigieg**
*   **Role:** Secretary of Transportation
*   **Dates:** February 3, 2021 – December 31, 2024
*   **Note:** Confirmed by the Senate and sworn in on February 3, 2021. He served through the end of 2024.
    *   *Clarification on Deputy Secretary:* While Buttigieg took paternity leave in late 2021, Deputy Secretary **Polly Trottenberg** managed day-to-day operations but did not officially assume the title of "Acting Secretary," as Buttigieg remained in office.
